newsitem.title: UK: Mortar attack casts new shadow over N.Irish talks.
newsitem.headline: Mortar attack casts new shadow over N.Irish talks.

text.p: The Irish Republican Army was blamed on Sunday for a mortar attack on a village police station as Northern Ireland's rival parties prepared for a new round of fraught peace talks.
Security sources said the outlawed guerrilla group were the prime suspects for the attack on the police post in Tempo in County Fermanagh, 80 miles (144 km) west of Belfast, on Saturday night.
"Two mortars were fired, one lodged in the station roof and one landed in the station yard," a police spokesman said. "Both failed to explode and were defused by army experts."

A sudden upsurge in IRA hostilities and suspected revenge attacks by pro-British Loyalist hardliners have deepened the pessimism surrounding talks on the future of the British-ruled province that restart on Monday.

The talks, under former U.S. senator George Mitchell, involve all the major parties except the IRA's Sinn Fein political arm who are excluded because the guerrillas refuse to call off a war against British rule.

British army bomb disposal officers moved in at first light to establish the precise cause of the Tempo blast. Security personnel said they thought a mortar had been fired from a van which then burst into flames outside the unoccupied station.
Police said no one was injured.

Although no group claimed immediate responsibility, security sources said it might be part of an escalating Irish Republican Army campaign which has heightened tension in the British province and promoted fears of new sectarian violence.
Until they declared a truce in September 1994, the IRA frequently fired mortars at police and army bases using launch tubes stored in vans.

Last week the IRA, which has fought a 27-year war to end British rule in Northern Ireland, admitted recent missile attacks on a security hut at Belfast's Courts of Justice and on an armoured car police patrol in Londonderry.
Security has been tightened across the province to combat an upsurge in IRA activity since shortly before Christmas amid fears of fresh attacks by pro-British Loyalist guerrillas.
Media reports have blamed them for two suspected revenge attacks on leading Catholic republicans who want creation of an all-Ireland state.

Loyalist politicians linked to the banned guerrillas say they will try to head off any attempt to expel them from the Belfast multi-party talks because of their failure to condemn the attacks blamed on Protestant extremists.
"We will resist attempts to remove us. We are not guilty," Loyalist politician David Ervine told Reuters.
Loyalists were given seats because a ceasefire the Protestant militia declared in October 1994 remained in force after the IRA ended their own ceasefire last February.

Mainstream Protestant "Unionist" politicians, who condemn guerrilla activity, say they will press Britain to state whether its intelligence agencies believe the recent attacks mark the end of the truce.

Protestant and Catholic moderate Nationalists want the IRA to declare an immediate truce but are deadlocked on when guerrillas should give up their arms in the event of one and on the timing of Sinn Fein's entry to the talks.

Political analysts say the talks are unlikely to make progress before a British general election, due by May at the latest, during which the parties will vie for Northern Ireland's 18 seats in the London parliament.
